**Editor's Note and Summary**

The Parivārapāḷi, the fifth text of the Vinaya Piṭaka, has been designated as the sixth text in the Buddha Jayanti Tripiṭaka text series. However, for ease of study of the text, when printing it together with the Sinhala translation while taking care to place footnotes in their proper positions, it was found that the text would become unwieldy to handle comfortably if kept as a single volume. For this reason, the portion of the Parivārapāḷi ending with the "Samathabheda" has been published as Section 1, in the year 1977 C.E.

The remainder of the text, beginning with the Bandhakapuccha and ending with the Nava Saṅgahavagga, is published here as Section 2 of the Parivārapāḷi. Whatever needs to be said regarding the Parivārapāḷi as a whole may be understood from the note written in the first section; therefore a separate note has not been written here. Readers are advised to consult that note.

At the invitation of the Lanka Buddhist Board (Lankā Bauddha Maṇḍalaya), the Parivārapāḷi was translated into the Sinhala language by the Venerable Polgahawela Vidyānandavardhana Mahā Nāyaka Thera, Pariveṇādhipati-Upādhyāya, Kakulandala-vihāra Sirirakkhita-nāyaka. Being a learned scholar well versed in the Dhamma and Vinaya, the Sinhala translation he completed in due course was revised, after examination of the Pāli text, by the learned elder monks of the present Tripiṭaka Compilation Board. The style of composition and the orthographic conventions here have also been employed in keeping with the tradition followed by the translator-monk himself, without departure.

I consider it a cause of great joy to all the Sinhala Buddhist people who wish for the continuance of the Sāsana that the Parivārapāḷi — a text of the greatest importance for the maintenance of discipline among the bhikkhus — has, through this translation into fluent Sinhala, been brought to publication. I wish that the virtuous members of the Lanka Buddhist Board, who took the lead in this meritorious undertaking, as well as all the learned persons engaged in the Department of Cultural Affairs, and the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka, may all be free from affliction through the merit of this Dhamma-gift.

May blessings be upon all beings!

With this,
Promoter of the Sāsana,

Labugama Lankānanda Thera
Chief Editor, Tripiṭaka Compilation Board

9th of June, 1979
Mahānāyaka Pariveṇārāmaya

**The Progressive Series (Ekuttarikā)**

**The Ones**

1. One should know the matter that gives rise to an offense; one should know the matter that does not give rise to an offense.

One should know an offense; one should know a non-offense.

One should know a light offense; one should know a heavy offense.

One should know an offense with remainder; one should know an offense without remainder.

One should know an offense that leads to confession; one should know an offense that does not lead to confession.

One should know an offense admitting of remedy; one should know an offense not admitting of remedy.

One should know an offense that leads to confession; one should know an offense that does not lead to confession.

One should know an offense that is an obstruction; one should know an offense that is not an obstruction.

One should know an offense to be disclosed as blameworthy; one should know an offense to be disclosed as blameless.

One should know an offense arising from an act; one should know an offense arising from a non-act; one should know an offense arising from both act and non-act.

One should know a prior offense; one should know a subsequent offense.

One should know the offense that falls between prior offenses; one should know the offense that falls between subsequent offenses.

One should know an offense which, once confessed, is reckoned as cleared; one should know an offense which, once confessed, is not so reckoned.

One should know what is to be disclosed; one should know what is not to be disclosed; one should know what, though not yet arisen, is still to be disclosed.

One should know what is to be disclosed in full; one should know what is to be disclosed only in part,

One should know what is to be disclosed in common; one should know what is to be disclosed not in common.

One should know what is to be disclosed to one side; one should know what is to be disclosed to both sides.

One should know a minor offense; one should know a non-minor offense.

8

**Parivāra Pāḷi – Ekuttarika (The Series Increasing by One)**

[An offense should be known as such by its basis] — an offense should be known as not [arising] from that basis.

A determined (niyata) offense should be known, an undetermined (aniyata) offense should be known.

The person who is the originator (of an offense) should be known; the person who is not the originator should be known.

The person who offends only occasionally should be known; the person who offends constantly should be known.

The accuser should be known; the accused should be known.

The person who accuses unlawfully should be known; the person who is accused unlawfully should be known.

The person who accuses lawfully should be known; the person who is accused lawfully should be known.

The confined person should be known; the unconfined person should be known.

The person liable to an offense should be known; the person not liable to an offense should be known.

The suspended person should be known; the unsuspended person should be known.

The expelled person should be known; the unexpelled person should be known.

The person of the same communion should be known; the person not of the same communion should be known.

"These things should be known" — thus [it is said].

The Ones (ekaka) have been shown.

—————

**Its summary:**

1. The doer, the offense, the light one, the one with remainder, the grave fault,
   rectification and confession, and the interim examinable procedure —

2. action and non-action, the prior, the interim, that which falls into the reckoning,
   the one in a normal state, the one who has not offended, [the matter of] the Omniscient One, and the retention of partial knowledge — all together —

3. the determined person, and the originator, the occasional offender, the accuser,
   the unlawful and the lawful [accuser and accused], the confined one, the one incapable [of offense], the suspended, the expelled,
   the one of equal [communion], and "these things" — all together, thus this was said.

---

1. "Rectification, confession, and the interim examinable procedure" — [variant reading in the] Ma, Ja, Saṃ [manuscripts].
2. "The Omniscient One's [matter] and the retention, together" — [variant in] Ma, Ja, Saṃ; "the normal state, non-occurrence, all in the retention, together" — [variant in the] Syā (Siamese manuscript).

**THE PAIRS**

1. There is an offense released by formal settlement; there is an offense not released by formal settlement.

There is an offense connected with attainment through view; there is an offense not connected with attainment through view.

There is an offense connected with what is proper; there is an offense connected with what is improper.

There is an offense connected with one's own requisites; there is an offense connected with another's requisites.

There is an offense connected with oneself as a person; there is an offense connected with another person.

By excluding one thing, one incurs a grave offense; by excluding another thing, one incurs a light offense.

By excluding one root-cause, one incurs a grave offense; by excluding another root-cause, one incurs a light offense.

There is an offense incurred by one standing on the ground, not by one standing in the air; there is an offense incurred by one standing in the air, not by one standing on the ground.

There is an offense incurred by one going out, not by one entering; there is an offense incurred by one entering, not by one going out.

There is an offense incurred at the very start [of an act]; there is an offense incurred not at the start.

There is an offense incurred all at once; there is an offense not incurred all at once.

There is an offense incurred by one who causes [it] to be done; there is an offense not incurred by one who causes [it] to be done.

There is an offense incurred by one who gives; there is an offense not incurred by one who gives.

There is an offense incurred by one who shows; there is an offense not incurred by one who shows.

There is an offense incurred by one who accepts; there is an offense not incurred by one who accepts.

There is an offense incurred by one who uses; there is an offense not incurred by one who uses.

There is an offense incurred at night, not by day; there is an offense incurred by day, not at night.

There is an offense incurred in a remote place; there is an offense not incurred in a remote place.

**[continuing from the previous section]**

By eight ways, one who knows commits an offense; by eight ways, one who does not know does not commit an offense.

By eight ways, one who perceives commits an offense; by eight ways, one who does not perceive does not commit an offense.

By eight ways, one who bears it in mind commits an offense; by eight ways, one who does not bear it in mind does not commit an offense.

**2.** Two Observance days: the fourteenth and the fifteenth.

Two Invitation days: the fourteenth and the fifteenth.

Two formal acts: the act by announcement (apalokana-kamma), the act by motion (ñatti-kamma). And again two other formal acts: the act by motion-and-one-proclamation (ñattidutiya-kamma), the act by motion-and-three-proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma).

Two failures of a formal act: the failure of the act by announcement, the failure of the act by motion. And again two other failures of a formal act: the failure of the act by motion-and-one-proclamation, the failure of the act by motion-and-three-proclamations.

Two faults of a formal act: the fault of the act by announcement, the fault of the act by motion. And again two other faults of a formal act: the fault of the act by motion-and-one-proclamation, the fault of the act by motion-and-three-proclamations.

Two successes of a formal act: the success of the act by announcement, the success of the act by motion. And again two other successes of a formal act: the success of the act by motion-and-one-proclamation, the success of the act by motion-and-three-proclamations.

Two marks of one of different communion: he makes himself of different communion by himself, or the Order suspends him — either for not acknowledging (an offense), or for not making amends for it,

**Section Summary – the Nineteenth**

The gain of two kinds of persons should not be given up as forfeited: it is not proper [to deal thus] with either the shameless one or the conscientious one.

The gain of two kinds of persons should be given up as forfeited: it is proper [to deal thus] with either the foolish one or the conscientious one.

The persons who [may] commit an offense without a companion: a bhikkhu, or one who has become defeated (pārājika).

The persons who [may] commit an offense with a companion: a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī.

THE GREAT SECTION ON LEGAL QUESTIONS

1. There are four legal questions: the legal question of dispute, the legal question of accusation, the legal question of offense, the legal question of duty. These are the four legal questions.

How many settlements are there for these four legal questions? There are ten settlements for these four legal questions: for the legal question of dispute, two settlements; for the legal question of accusation, four settlements; for the legal question of offense, three settlements; for the legal question of duty, one settlement. These are the ten settlements for these four legal questions.

2. By how many means of settlement is the legal question of dispute settled? By how many means of settlement is the legal question of accusation settled? By how many means of settlement is the legal question of offense settled? By how many means of settlement is the legal question of duty settled?

The legal question of dispute is settled by two means of settlement. The legal question of accusation is settled by four means of settlement. The legal question of offense is settled by three means of settlement. The legal question of duty is settled by one means of settlement.

3. How many settlements are there, by how many factors do settlements come about, possessed of how many qualities does a person settle a legal question, how many persons, in settling a legal question, commit an offense?

There are seven settlements; they come about through ten factors. Possessed of four qualities, a person settles a legal question; four persons, in settling a legal question, commit an offense.

4. What are the seven settlements? An act not done, a wrongly done act, an act that must be done again; a matter not withdrawn, wrongly withdrawn, a matter that must be withdrawn again; a matter not decided, wrongly decided, a matter that must be decided again; a matter not settled, wrongly settled, a matter that must be settled again — these are the seven settlements.

5. By what ten factors do settlements come about: a legal question that did not arise there is not settled; a legal question that did not arise there, even if wrongly settled, is not [properly] settled; a legal question arising in another place is settled; a legal question arising in another place, if wrongly settled, is [still not properly] settled; a legal question not brought there is not settled; a legal question not brought there, if wrongly settled, is not [properly] settled; it is settled by a verdict given in the presence [of the parties]; by a verdict of past insanity; by the procedure against persistent wrongdoing; by covering over as with grass. By these ten factors do settlements come about.

On the Origins of Legal Matters

1. Of what is the legal matter concerning disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa) the source, of what the origin, of what the cause, of what the arising, of what the concurrence, of what the coming together? Of what is the legal matter concerning accusations (anuvādādhikaraṇa) the source, of what the origin, of what the cause, of what the arising, of what the concurrence, of what the coming together? The legal matter concerning disputes has dispute as its source, dispute as its origin, dispute as its cause, dispute as its arising, dispute as its concurrence, dispute as its coming together. The legal matter concerning accusations has accusation as its source, accusation as its origin, accusation as its cause, accusation as its arising, accusation as its concurrence, accusation as its coming together. The legal matter concerning offenses has offense as its source, offense as its origin, offense as its cause, offense as its arising, offense as its concurrence, offense as its coming together. The legal matter concerning duties has duty as its source, duty as its origin, duty as its cause, duty as its arising, duty as its concurrence, duty as its coming together.

2. Of what is the legal matter concerning disputes the source, of what the origin, of what the cause, of what the arising, of what the concurrence, of what the coming together? Of what is the legal matter concerning accusations –...– the legal matter concerning offenses –...– the legal matter concerning duties the source, of what the origin, of what the cause, of what the arising, of what the concurrence, of what the coming together?

**Parivāra Pāḷi – On the Classification of Adjudications**

A dispute-adjudication has cause as its source, cause as its origin, cause as its birthplace, cause as its wellspring, cause as its requisite condition, cause as its arising. An accusation-adjudication — etc. — an offense-adjudication — etc. — a duty-adjudication has cause as its source, cause as its origin, cause as its birthplace, cause as its wellspring, cause as its requisite condition, cause as its arising.

**3.** What is the source of a dispute-adjudication? What is its origin? What is its birthplace? What is its wellspring? What is its requisite condition? What is its arising? An accusation-adjudication — etc. — an offense-adjudication — etc. — what is the source of a duty-adjudication? What is its origin? What is its birthplace? What is its wellspring? What is its requisite condition? What is its arising?

A dispute-adjudication has contention as its source, contention as its origin, contention as its birthplace, contention as its wellspring, contention as its requisite condition, contention as its arising. An accusation-adjudication — etc. — an offense-adjudication — etc. — a duty-adjudication has contention as its source, contention as its origin, contention as its birthplace, contention as its wellspring, contention as its requisite condition, contention as its arising.

**Statement of the Roots of Adjudications**

**1.** How many roots have the four adjudications? Thirty-three are their roots.
How many originations have the four adjudications? Thirty-three are their originations.

**2.** Which are the thirty-three roots of the four adjudications?
The dispute-adjudication has twelve roots; the accusation-adjudication has fourteen roots; the offense-adjudication has six roots; the duty-adjudication has one root, it is said. These are the thirty-three roots of the four adjudications.

**3.** Which are the thirty-three originations of the four adjudications?
The dispute-adjudication has the eighteen grounds for schism as its originations; the accusation-adjudication has the four kinds of failure as its originations; the offense-adjudication has the seven classes of offense as its originations;¹ the duty-adjudication has the four [kinds of formal] acts as its originations. These are the thirty-three originations of the four adjudications.

**Offenses Arising by Reason of Adjudication**

**1.** Is a dispute-adjudication itself an offense? A dispute-adjudication is not an offense.
But could one, by reason of a dispute-adjudication, commit an offense? Yes — by reason of a dispute-adjudication one could commit an offense.

112 Parivāra Pāḷi – Division of Legal Cases (Adhikaraṇabheda)

How many offences does one commit owing to a dispute-case (vivādādhikaraṇa)? Owing to a dispute-case one commits two offences: for those who are fully ordained, an offence of expiation (pācittiya) arises from insulting; for those not fully ordained, an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) arises from insulting. Owing to a dispute-case, one commits these two offences.

2. Of these offences, to how many of the four kinds of failure do they belong? Of the four legal cases, which legal case [do they belong to]? Of the seven classes of offence, by how many classes of offence are they included? Of the six origins of offence, by how many origins do they arise? By how many legal cases, in how many kinds of knowledge, by how many means of settlement are they settled?

Of these offences, they belong to one of the four kinds of failure: failure in conduct. Of the four legal cases, it is the legal case concerning an offence. Of the seven classes of offence, they are included by two classes of offence: sometimes by the class of pācittiya offence, sometimes by the class of dukkaṭa offence. Of the six origins of offence, they arise by three origins. By one legal case: the legal case concerning business. In two kinds of knowledge: by the all-inclusive knowledge, in the presence of the person. By two means they are settled: sometimes by verdict in the presence [of the parties] together with acknowledgement of the offence, sometimes by verdict in the presence together with the decision of the majority.

3. Is a legal case concerning an accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa) [composed] of an offence or of a non-offence? A legal case concerning an accusation is not [itself] an offence.

But does one commit an offence owing to a legal case concerning an accusation? Yes, one may commit an offence owing to a legal case concerning an accusation.

How many offences does one commit owing to a legal case concerning an accusation? Owing to a legal case concerning an accusation, one commits three offences: for one who charges a monk with a baseless pārājika matter, an offence of saṅghādisesa; for one who charges with a baseless saṅghādisesa matter, an offence of pācittiya; for one who charges with a baseless failure in conduct, an offence of dukkaṭa. Owing to a legal case concerning an accusation, one commits these three offences.

4. Of these offences, to how many of the four kinds of failure do they belong? Of the four legal cases, which legal case? Of the seven classes of offence, by how many classes are they included? Of the six origins of offence, by how many origins do they arise? By how many legal cases, in how many kinds of knowledge, by how many means are they settled?

Of these offences, they belong to two of the four kinds of failure: sometimes failure in virtue, sometimes failure in conduct. Of the four legal cases, it is the legal case concerning an offence. Of the seven classes of offence, they are included by three classes: sometimes by the class of saṅghādisesa offence, sometimes by the class of pācittiya offence, sometimes by the class of dukkaṭa offence. Of the six origins of offence, they arise by three origins. [illegible] By one legal case: the legal case concerning business.

**114. Parivāra Pāḷi – Enumeration of Legal Issues (Adhikaraṇagaṇanā)**

In one door: in the presence of the Sangha. It is settled by two means of settlement: by a verdict given face to face, and by acting on acknowledgement. Whatever offenses there are, they fall under one legal issue, not under four legal issues. In three doors: in the midst of the Sangha, in the midst of a group, and in the presence of an individual. These are settled by two means: in one case by a face-to-face verdict together with acting on acknowledgement, in another case by a face-to-face verdict together with [recollection].

5. An offense-legal-issue in relation to what has occurred: an offense-legal-issue is where an offense has occurred.

Now does an offense arise because of an offense-legal-issue? Yes, an offense arises because of an offense-legal-issue.

Because of an offense-legal-issue, what offenses arise? Because of an offense-legal-issue these four offenses arise: a monk who, knowing it, conceals a pārājika matter¹ incurs an offense entailing pārājika; one who, being in doubt, conceals it incurs an offense of thullaccaya; a monk who conceals a genuine saṅghādisesa incurs an offense of pācittiya; one who conceals a breach of conduct incurs an offense of dukkaṭa. Because of an offense-legal-issue, these four offenses arise.

6. Of whatever offenses there are, how many kinds of breach are there to be found? Of whatever legal issues there are, how many legal issues are there? Of all the groupings of offenses, how many such groupings are there? Of all the assemblies [that deal with offenses], how many assemblies and how many gatherings are there? How many legal issues, in how many doors, and by how many means of settlement are they settled?

Of whatever offenses there are, two kinds of breach are to be found: breach of virtue and breach of conduct. Of all legal issues, there is the offense-legal-issue. Of all groupings of offenses, there are four groupings: the group of offenses entailing pārājika, the group of offenses entailing saṅghādisesa, the group of offenses entailing pācittiya, and the group of offenses entailing dukkaṭa. Of all the assemblies dealing with offenses, there is one assembly: it is carried out by the Sangha, by a group, or by an individual. Whatever offense there is, whatever is not incurred, it belongs to no legal issue, to no door, to no means of settlement — of whatever offenses there are. Whatever offenses are obtained fall under one legal issue, not under four legal issues. In three doors: in the midst of the Sangha, in the midst of a group, in the presence of an individual. They are settled by two means: in one case by a face-to-face verdict together with acting on acknowledgement, in another case by a face-to-face verdict together with recollection.

7. A duty-legal-issue in relation to what is to be done: a duty-legal-issue is where a duty is to be carried out.

Now does an offense arise because of a duty-legal-issue? Yes, an offense arises because of a duty-legal-issue.

**[Due to the legal question of function]**

Due to the cause of a legal-question-of-function, how many kinds of offense come to be incurred? Due to the cause of a legal-question-of-function, five kinds of offense come to be incurred:

For one of double sex (or: one being formally admonished) who, up to the motion and the formal act of admonition, does not give up [the matter], there is an offense of wrong-doing; with two formal proclamations [of the motion], an offense of grave matter; at the completion of the formal proclamation, an offense entailing defeat.

For one who follows a schismatic who, up to the motion and the formal act of admonition, does not give up [the matter], there is an offense requiring a formal meeting of the Order; for one of evil view who, up to the motion and the formal act of admonition, does not give up [the matter], there is an offense to be confessed.

**[Legal Issues (Adhikaraṇa) and their interconnections]**

**1.** A dispute-issue (vivādādhikaraṇa) may give rise to an accusation-issue (anuvādādhikaraṇa); it may give rise to an offense-issue (āpattādhikaraṇa); it may give rise to a procedural issue (kiccādhikaraṇa).

Disputing, one accuses — this is the accusation-issue. Accusing, one commits an offense — this is the offense-issue. Because of that offense, the Sangha carries out a formal act — this is the procedural issue. Thus, with a dispute-issue as condition, there comes to be an accusation-issue, there comes to be an offense-issue, there comes to be a procedural issue.

**2.** An accusation-issue may give rise to an offense-issue, may give rise to a procedural issue, may give rise to a dispute-issue.

An accusation-issue is not [in itself] an offense-issue, is not a procedural issue, is not a dispute-issue. Yet, with an accusation-issue as condition, there comes to be an offense-issue, there comes to be a procedural issue, there comes to be a dispute-issue. How is this?

Here, monks accuse a monk of a failure in virtue, or a failure in conduct, or a failure in view, or a failure in livelihood. Whatever in this connection is accusation, accusing, following up with accusation, pursuing, keeping to the point, reminding, prompting — this is called the accusation-issue.

With the accusation-issue as condition, the Sangha disputes — this is the dispute-issue. Disputing, one accuses — this is the accusation-issue. Accusing, one commits an offense — this is the offense-issue. Because of that offense, the Sangha carries out a formal act — this is the procedural issue. Thus, with the accusation-issue as condition, there comes to be an offense-issue, there comes to be a procedural issue, there comes to be a dispute-issue.

**3.** An offense-issue may give rise to a procedural issue, may give rise to a dispute-issue, may give rise to an accusation-issue.

An offense-issue is not [in itself] a procedural issue, is not a dispute-issue, is not an accusation-issue. Yet, with an offense-issue as condition, there comes to be a procedural issue, there comes to be a dispute-issue, there comes to be an accusation-issue. How is this?

Whatever belongs to the five classes of offense is an offense-issue; whatever belongs to the seven classes of offense is an offense-issue — this is called the offense-issue.

With the offense-issue as condition, the Sangha disputes — this is the dispute-issue. Disputing, one accuses — this is the accusation-issue. Accusing, one commits an offense — this is the offense-issue. Because of that offense, the Sangha carries out a formal act — this is the procedural issue. Thus, with the offense-issue as condition, there comes to be a procedural issue, there comes to be a dispute-issue, there comes to be an accusation-issue.

**4.** A procedural issue may give rise to a dispute-issue, may give rise to an accusation-issue, may give rise to an offense-issue.

A procedural issue is not [in itself] a dispute-issue, is not an accusation-issue, is not an offense-issue. Yet, with a procedural issue as condition, there comes to be a dispute-issue, there comes to be an accusation-issue, there comes to be an offense-issue. How is this?

Whatever business is to be done by the Sangha through a formal act — an act of announcement (apalokanakamma), an act with a motion (ñattikamma), an act with a motion and one proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma), an act with a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatutthakamma) — this is called the procedural issue.

With the procedural issue as condition, the Sangha disputes — this is the dispute-issue. Disputing, one accuses — this is the accusation-issue. Accusing, one commits an offense — this is the offense-issue. Because of that offense, the Sangha carries out a formal act — this is the procedural issue. Thus, with the procedural issue as condition, there comes to be a dispute-issue, there comes to be an accusation-issue, there comes to be an offense-issue.

**The Conduct of the Accuser and Others**

1. The accuser should proceed with care. The accused should proceed with care. The Sangha should proceed with care. The investigator should proceed with care.

"The accuser should proceed with care": the accuser, having established himself in five qualities, should accuse the other person: "I will speak at the right time, not at the wrong time; I will speak what is true, not what is untrue; I will speak gently, not harshly; I will speak what is beneficial, not what is useless; I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of hatred." Thus should the accuser proceed.

"The accused should proceed with care": the accused should proceed established in two things: truthfulness and freedom from anger. Thus should the accused proceed.

"The Sangha should proceed with care": the Sangha should know what has been examined and what has not been examined. Thus should the Sangha proceed.

"The investigator should proceed with care": the investigator should settle that dispute by whatever means — whether by the Dhamma, by the Vinaya, or by the Teacher's instruction — through which that dispute can be settled. Thus should the investigator proceed.

**14. What is called "going by bias through delusion" (mohāgati)?**

One who goes by bias through delusion goes by bias in this way: he goes by the sway of attachment, by the sway of hatred, by the sway of delusion, by the sway of fear. Overcome by delusion, with mind obsessed by delusion, he declares the non-Dhamma to be Dhamma, and declares the Dhamma to be non-Dhamma — ... — he declares what is not an offence to be an offence, and declares what is an offence to be not an offence.

Going by bias through delusion in these eighteen distinguishable ways, he is one who has fallen into bias. For the sake of that bias he brings harm to many people, unhappiness to many people, and works for the detriment, harm, and suffering of gods and men. Going by bias through delusion in these eighteen distinguishable ways, he brings disrepute on himself, becomes blameworthy, and is censured by the wise, and much demerit is produced. This is how one who goes by bias through delusion goes by bias through delusion.

**15. What is called "going by bias through desire" (chandāgati)?**

One who goes by bias through desire goes by bias in this way: thinking, "this one is dependent on me for robes, or dependent on me for alms-food, or dependent on me for lodging, or dependent on me for medicines," or thinking, "this one is my preceptor, or my teacher's associate, or my pupil, or my fellow pupil, or my kinsman, or my blood relation" — swayed by desire for that person, he declares the non-Dhamma to be Dhamma, and declares the Dhamma to be non-Dhamma; he declares the non-Vinaya to be Vinaya, and declares the Vinaya to be non-Vinaya; he declares what was not spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata to have been spoken and uttered by him, and declares what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata to have not been spoken and uttered by him; he declares what was not practised by the Tathāgata to have been practised by him, and declares what was practised by the Tathāgata to have not been practised by him; he declares what was not laid down by the Tathāgata to have been laid down by him, and declares what was laid down by the Tathāgata to have not been laid down by him; he declares a non-offence to be an offence, and declares an offence to be a non-offence; he declares a light offence to be grave, and declares a grave offence to be light; he declares an offence with remainder to be without remainder, and declares an offence without remainder to be with remainder; he declares a coarse offence to be not coarse, and declares a not-coarse offence to be coarse.

Going by bias through desire in these eighteen distinguishable ways, he brings disrepute on himself, becomes blameworthy, and is censured by the wise, and much demerit is produced. Declaring non-Dhamma as "non-Dhamma" — ... — declaring a serious offense as "a serious offense" — ... — declaring a non-serious offense as "a non-serious offense" — ... — thus he inspires confidence in a matter that should inspire confidence.

26. How does one of a small following look down on the other faction? Here, someone, thinking, "I am of a small faction, of a small following, yet I do have a following; but this one — he has no small faction, no small following — in fact, he has no following at all!" — looking down on the other out of this conceit, declares non-Dhamma as "Dhamma," declares Dhamma as "non-Dhamma" — ... — declares a serious offense as "a non-serious offense," declares a non-serious offense as "a serious offense." Thus one of a small following looks down on the other faction.

27. How does one who is very learned look down on one of little learning? Here, someone, thinking, "I am very learned, a holder of what has been handed down, a keeper of what has been handed down; but this one is of little learning, has retained little of what has been handed down, has retained little of the Vinaya" — looking down on the other out of this conceit, declares non-Dhamma as "Dhamma"...

28. How an elder overpowers a junior: Here a certain elder is one of long standing, intelligent, wise. Thinking, "This junior is of little wisdom, of little learning, of little repute; his word will carry no weight" — with this thought he overpowers him: he declares non-Dhamma as Dhamma, declares Dhamma as non-Dhamma —and so on— declares a serious offense as a non-serious offense, declares a non-serious offense as a serious offense. **The Questioning by the Investigating Officer**

The investigating officer should question the expert in the Vinaya thus: "Friend, that fault which is seen in this monk — in what is it seen? Is it seen in a failure of virtue, is it seen in a failure of conduct, is it seen in a failure of view?"

If he should answer thus: "It is seen in a failure of virtue, or it is seen in a failure of conduct, or it is seen in a failure of view" —

he should then be asked: "But do you know what a failure of virtue is? Do you know what a failure of conduct is? Do you know what a failure of view is?"

If he should answer thus: "I do indeed know, friend, what a failure of virtue is; I know what a failure of conduct is; I know what a failure of view is" —

he should then be asked: "But which, then, is his failure of virtue? Which is his failure of conduct? Which is his failure of view?"

**15.** Then that bhikkhu who has spread the kathina robe should approach a single bhikkhu, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, raise his joined palms, and should address him thus: "Friend, the kathina robe is being spread for the Sangha; it is a lawful spreading of the kathina robe; please give your approval." Then that bhikkhu who approves should likewise arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, raise his joined palms, and should reply thus: "Friend, the kathina robe is being spread for the Sangha; it is a lawful spreading of the kathina robe; I approve."

Does the Sangha spread the kathina robe? Does a group spread the kathina robe? Does an individual spread the kathina robe? — It is not the Sangha that spreads the kathina robe, nor a group that spreads the kathina robe; it is an individual who spreads the kathina robe. Even though it is not the Sangha that spreads the kathina robe, nor a group that spreads the kathina robe, but an individual who spreads it: for the Sangha the kathina robe remains unspread, for the group it remains unspread, for the individual it becomes spread.

Does the Sangha recite the Pātimokkha? Does a group recite the Pātimokkha? Does an individual recite the Pātimokkha? — It is not the Sangha that recites the Pātimokkha, nor a group that recites the Pātimokkha; it is an individual who recites the Pātimokkha. Even though it is not the Sangha that recites the Pātimokkha, nor a group that recites the Pātimokkha, but an individual who recites it: for the Sangha the Pātimokkha remains unrecited, for the group it remains unrecited, for the individual it becomes recited. Yet through the concord of the Sangha, the concord of the group, and the recitation by the individual: for the Sangha the Pātimokkha becomes recited, for the group it becomes recited, for the individual it becomes recited.

In just the same way, it is not the Sangha that spreads the kathina robe, nor a group that spreads the kathina robe; it is an individual who spreads it. Yet through the approval of the Sangha, the approval of the group, and the spreading by the individual: for the Sangha the kathina robe becomes spread, for the group it becomes spread, for the individual it becomes spread.

**6.** "With how many qualities, then, possessed of, should a formal act be performed against a monk?"

A formal act should be performed, Upāli, against a monk possessed of five qualities. What five? He is shameless; he is foolish; he is of bad character; he is fallen in conduct; and he is fallen in livelihood. These, Upāli, are the five qualities possessed of which a formal act should be performed against a monk.

**7.** Furthermore, Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a monk possessed of five [other] qualities. What five? He is unvirtuous and fallen in virtue; he is unrestrained and fallen in conduct; he holds extreme views and is fallen in view; he is of wrong livelihood; and he is fallen in livelihood. These, Upāli, are the five qualities possessed of which a formal act should be performed against a monk.

**8.** Furthermore, Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a monk possessed of five [other] qualities. What five? He is possessed of bodily frivolity; he is possessed of verbal frivolity; he is possessed of both bodily and verbal frivolity; he is fallen in view; and he is fallen in livelihood. These, Upāli, are the five qualities possessed of which a formal act should be performed against a monk.

These, Upāli, are the five qualities possessed of which a formal act should be performed against a monk.

**11.** Furthermore, Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a monk possessed of five [other] qualities. What five? **6.** "How many qualities, lord, must a monk possess in order to be of great help to monks engaged in a legal question?"

"Upāli, a monk possessing five qualities is of great help to monks engaged in a legal question. What five? He stands firm in the discipline, not to be shaken; he is capable, by reasoned talk, of convincing, informing, inciting, and gladdening either party. These, Upāli, are the five qualities which a monk should possess in order to be of great help to monks engaged in a legal question.

**7. The Section on False Speech**

**1.** "What, venerable sir, is called false speech?"

"There are these five, Upāli. What five? There is false speech that is a pārājika offense, there is false speech that is a saṅghādisesa offense, there is false speech that is a thullaccaya offense, there is false speech that is a pācittiya offense, there is false speech that is a dukkaṭa offense. These, Upāli, are the five kinds of false speech."

**2.** "How many qualities, venerable sir, must a bhikkhu of the same communion possess so that, when he says to a bhikkhu who is stopping the uposatha or the pavāraṇā, 'Enough, bhikkhu, do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not contend, do not litigate,' the uposatha or the pavāraṇā may, on the strength of that very statement, still be carried out as before?"

"Five, Upāli. Possessing five qualities, when a bhikkhu of the same communion says to a bhikkhu who is stopping the uposatha or the pavāraṇā, 'Enough, bhikkhu, do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not contend, do not litigate,' the uposatha or the pavāraṇā may, on the strength of that very statement, still be carried out as before. What five? He is without shame, he is foolish, he is not of proper conduct, his speech is governed by mere assertion, not by what he has actually seen. These, Upāli, are the five qualities possessing which, when a bhikkhu of the same communion says to a bhikkhu who is stopping the uposatha or the pavāraṇā, 'Enough, bhikkhu, do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not contend, do not litigate,' the uposatha or the pavāraṇā may, on the strength of that very statement, still be carried out as before.

Again, Upāli, possessing another five qualities, when a bhikkhu of the same communion says to a bhikkhu who is stopping the uposatha or the pavāraṇā, 'Enough, bhikkhu, do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not contend, do not litigate,' the uposatha or the pavāraṇā may, on the strength of that very statement, still be carried out as before. What five? He is one whose bodily conduct is impure, he is one whose verbal conduct is impure, he is one whose livelihood is impure, he is foolish and inexperienced, he is a maker of quarrels and a maker of disputes. These, Upāli, are the five qualities possessing which, when a bhikkhu of the same communion says to a bhikkhu who is stopping the uposatha or the pavāraṇā, 'Enough, bhikkhu, do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not contend, do not litigate,' the uposatha or the pavāraṇā may, on the strength of that very statement, still be carried out as before."

**3.** "How many qualities, venerable sir, [disqualify a bhikkhu], such that exhortation should not be given to a bhikkhu of the same communion?"

"Five, Upāli. Possessing five qualities, exhortation should not be given to a bhikkhu of the same communion. What five? He does not know an offense as an offense, he does not know a light offense as light, he does not know an offense with remainder and one without remainder, he does not know a coarse offense and one that is not coarse, he does not know an offense that can be remedied and one that cannot be remedied. These, Upāli, are the five qualities possessing which exhortation should not be given to a bhikkhu of the same communion."

**280 — Upāli's Fives (Pañcaka)**

Upāli, a monk endowed with five qualities should have a charge brought against him. What five? He is one who has actually fallen into an offense; he is one who habitually repeats an offense; he is one who, through association [with others], falls into an offense; he is one who is weak and feeble and falls into an offense; he is one whose offense is either reparable or irreparable. Endowed with these five qualities, Upāli, a monk should have a charge brought against him.

**4.** In how many ways, then, does a monk fall into an offense?

In five ways, Upāli, does a monk fall into an offense. What five? Through shamelessness, through ignorance, through being overcome by scruples, through perceiving the unallowable as allowable, and through perceiving the allowable as unallowable. By these five, Upāli, a monk falls into an offense.

In another five ways too, Upāli, a monk falls into an offense. What five? Through not having seen, through not having heard, through coarseness [of mind], through uncertainty, and through lapse of mindfulness. By these five, Upāli, a monk falls into an offense.

**5.** What, then, are the perils?

There are five perils, Upāli. What five? The taking of life, taking what is not given, wrong conduct in sensual pleasures, false speech, and indulgence in liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that lead to heedlessness. These, Upāli, are the five perils.

**6.** What, then, are the abstinences?

There are five abstinences, Upāli. What five? Abstinence from taking life, abstinence from taking what is not given, abstinence from wrong conduct in sensual pleasures, abstinence from false speech, and abstinence from liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that lead to heedlessness. These, Upāli, are the five abstinences.

**7.** What, then, are the faculties?

There are five faculties, Upāli. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. These, Upāli, are the five faculties.

**8.** What, then, are the attainments?

There are five attainments, Upāli. What five? The attainment of faith, the attainment of virtue, the attainment of learning, the attainment of generosity, and the attainment of wisdom. These, Upāli, are the five attainments.

**[Section on Perils and Abstinences concluded.]**

"Upāli, these five are the unrighteous grounds concerning the Vinaya. Which five? **1. Kammavagga (Chapter on Formal Acts)**

1. There are four kinds of formal act: the act of announcement (*apalokana-kamma*), the motion-act (*ñatti-kamma*), the motion-and-second act (*ñatti-dutiya-kamma*), and the motion-and-fourth act (*ñatti-catuttha-kamma*). These four kinds of formal act are found in the Khandhaka on formal acts. These four kinds of formal act become defective in five ways: by reason of the basis (object), or by reason of the motion, or by reason of the announcement, or by reason of the boundary, or by reason of the assembly.

2. How do formal acts become defective by reason of the basis? An act which should be done in the presence [of the one concerned], one does in his absence — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. An act which should be done after questioning, one does without questioning — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. An act which should be done upon admission [of the offence], one does without such admission — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act.

To one who deserves the verdict of innocence through mindfulness (*sati-vinaya*), one gives instead the verdict of past unsoundness of mind (*amūḷha-vinaya*) — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. To one who deserves the verdict of past unsoundness of mind, one carries out instead the act of further punishment (*tassapāpiyyasikā-kamma*) — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. To one who deserves the act of further punishment, one carries out instead the act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*) — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. To one who deserves the act of censure, one carries out instead the act of guidance/subordination (*niyassa-kamma*) — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. To one who deserves the act of guidance, one carries out instead the act of banishment (*pabbājanīya-kamma*) — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. To one who deserves the act of banishment, one carries out instead the act of reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīya-kamma*) — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. To one who deserves the act of reconciliation, one carries out instead the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*) — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. To one who deserves the act of suspension, one grants him the matter [i.e., restores him] — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. In that matter, one draws him back to the origin — it is defective as to its basis, an unlawful act. [For one] to be drawn back to the origin... *[text continues on next page, remainder illegible/cut off]*

[continuing from the previous section, on acts defective "by faction" (vagga)]

One gives mānatta [improperly] — this is a factional act, an unlawful act.
One gives mānatta to one not worthy of mānatta — this is a factional act, an unlawful act.
One ordains one who is not a fit vessel [for ordination] — this is a factional act, an unlawful act.
One holds the Uposatha on a day that is not an Uposatha day — this is a factional act, an unlawful act.
One holds the Pavāraṇā [when it is] not the time for Pavāraṇā — this is a factional act, an unlawful act.
Thus is an act known to be defective through being factional.

**3.** How is an act known to be defective through "having a companion" (sadutiyaka)? By five ways is an act known to be defective through sadutiyaka: one does not take account of the faction, one does not take account of the individual, one does not take account of the person, one does not take account of the companion, one sets [the proper companion] aside and appoints [another as] companion. By these five ways is an act known to be defective through sadutiyaka.

**4.** How is an act known to be defective through [faulty] announcement (anussavana)? By five ways is an act known to be defective through faulty announcement: one does not take account of the faction, one does not take account of the individual, one does not take account of the person, one omits the announcement, one announces at the wrong time. By these five ways is an act known to be defective through faulty announcement.

**5.** How is an act known to be defective through the boundary (sīmā)? By eleven ways is an act known to be defective through the boundary: one marks out a boundary too small, one marks out a boundary too large, one marks out a boundary with broken landmarks, one marks out a boundary with a shadow as landmark, one marks out a boundary without landmarks, one marks out a boundary outside [the proper limits], one marks out a boundary on a riverbank, one marks out a boundary on the sea, one marks out a boundary on a natural lake, one makes a boundary overlap another boundary, one encloses a boundary within another boundary. By these eleven ways is an act known to be defective through the boundary.

**6.** How is an act known to be defective through the assembly (parisā)? By twelve ways is an act known to be defective through the assembly: in an act requiring the agreement of all present — as many bhikkhus as are fit to take part in that act have not come, the consent of those absent through illness has not been brought, and those present do object — [the act is defective]. In an act requiring [a quorum of] four — likewise, as many bhikkhus as are fit to take part in that act have not come, the consent of those absent through illness has not been brought, and those present do object. In an act requiring [a quorum of] five — ... In an act requiring [a quorum of] ten — ... In an act requiring [a quorum of] twenty — likewise, as many bhikkhus as are fit to take part in that act have not come, the consent of those absent through illness has not been brought, and those present do object. By these twelve ways is an act known to be defective through the assembly.

10. How does one understand an act [to be defective] by reason of the motion? By these five ways one understands an act [to be defective] by reason of the proclamation.

2. He had this concise treatise on the Vinaya written down, well composed, for the ease and happiness of the pupils.

3. The Parivāra expounds the Vinaya together with its particulars and its characteristics, matching doctrine with doctrine, so that each teaching accords with the other.

4. He surrounded the Teaching with the Parivāra as the ocean surrounds Jambudīpa; without the Parivāra, how could the meaning of the Dhamma-Vinaya be known?

5. The matters, together with the offences, with those who commit them and those who do not, should be seen, both in brief and in detail, by one versed in the ways of the world.

6. As a great physician, skilled in medicine, cures disease stage by stage by means of the fitting remedy,

7. As the sun, surrounded by its rays, together with its proper measure, dispels darkness step by step — so too this most excellent Vinaya shines forth in full through the Parivāra.
